scenes.heading: defer, panic & recover
scenes.narration: In the next minute, let's unpack Go's trio for cleanup and last-resort failure handling: defer, panic, and recover.

scenes.heading: What each keyword does
items: defer schedules a call to run when the function returns
panic stops normal flow and unwinds the stack
recover, inside a defer, catches a panic and resumes
scenes.narration: Think of these as everyday hygiene plus a rare emergency tool. defer registers a call that runs when the surrounding function returns, whether normally or via panic, which makes it perfect for cleanup. panic abandons normal control flow and unwinds the goroutine's stack. recover, called inside a deferred function, catches that panic and lets the function return normally instead of crashing.

scenes.heading: How a panic unwinds
steps: Deferred calls run in each frame, LIFO
A deferred recover halts the unwinding
No recover means the program crashes
scenes.narration: When panic fires, the runtime stops normal execution and walks up the goroutine frame by frame, running each frame's deferred calls in last-in-first-out order. If a deferred function calls recover, the runtime marks the panic handled and that function returns normally. If the panic reaches the top with no recover, the whole process crashes and prints a stack trace.

scenes.heading: Recover-to-error at a boundary
scenes.narration: Here is the idiomatic boundary pattern. Because err is a named return, the deferred closure can overwrite it. When b is zero, the division panics, the closure's recover returns the panic value, and we convert it into an ordinary error. The caller gets a value to handle rather than a crash. Note that recover only works when called directly inside a deferred function, in the same goroutine.

scenes.text: defer for cleanup; reserve panic/recover for truly exceptional cases and boundary recovery — always log recovered panics.
scenes.narration: The takeaway: reach for defer constantly to guarantee cleanup, but treat panic and recover as heavy tools, not exceptions. Recover at boundaries like an HTTP handler so one bad request returns a five hundred instead of crashing the server, and always log the recovered panic so the underlying bug still gets fixed.
